case_study_insert.main_stem: Zyloft Learning (ZYL) is a private limited company in the e-learning software sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2016 by Aisha Rahman, the business sells AI-tutoring and adaptive-assessment subscriptions to colleges and employers and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. ZYL plans to invest $680,000 in an AI-tutoring platform with adaptive assessments, financed by a $420,000 bank loan and $260,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $252,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.00 a unit and a selling price of $10.60, and currently produces 70,000 units a year. ZYL faces two problems: content-error complaints have risen, and labour turnover among instructional designers has reached 11%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Market Research Report — Q3 2025: A survey of 560 learners and tutors found 63% would upgrade to the AI-tutoring platform within 12 months, and 54% cited adaptive assessments as the main reason. 40% first heard of ZYL through social media. Course-completion rates improved from 64% to 71%, and platform uptime was 98.9%. Content errors reported fell from 38 to 19 a month after a review, though complaints from colleges remain. 22 of 40 staff are engineers; on-the-job training on the tutoring codebase runs weekly, while off-the-job AI-certification courses at the tech college cost $1,100 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Zyloft Learning for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Technology Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing the cost of variable-rate borrowing for education technology firms. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $12.35 to $13.14 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across support and administration teams. (3) Hosting and bandwidth costs rose 10.2% year-on-year, technology inflation is running at 5.5%, and business spending on e-learning software grew 12.3% over the same period.

questions.question_text: ZYL plans to fund part of its $680,000 AI-tutoring platform with a $420,000 bank loan and $260,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for ZYL of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest and no fixed repayment timetable, protecting cash flow while ZYL already has $252,000 of fixed costs a year and a contribution of $5.60 a unit ($10.60 − $5.00). With interest payable rising from $17,000 to $28,000 in Appendix 2, using $260,000 of internal funds instead of extra debt leaves cash to fix the content errors still reported by colleges and to reduce the 11% designer turnover, defending the $680,000 investment.

Point 2: Internal funding avoids lender covenants and collateral over ZYL's assets, so the AI-tutoring platform cannot be put at risk if uptake among the 560 surveyed learners and tutors falls short of the 63% intending to upgrade. It also keeps control with Aisha Rahman and the flat, democratic team. The trade-off is that $260,000 of reserves is no longer available if hosting costs keep rising by 10.2%, leaving a thinner buffer for the 11% turnover.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to ZYL's costs, reserves and funding decision.

questions.question_text: ZYL is launching its AI-tutoring platform. Consider advertising in education trade journals, social-media campaigns aimed at learners, or partnerships with employers offering staff training. Which should ZYL choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Education trade-journal advertising: Journals reach college buyers directly and give ZYL credibility for adaptive assessments, which 54% of the 560 surveyed learners and tutors cite as the main reason to upgrade. However, circulation is small, lead times are long, and print adverts cannot demonstrate the product, which limits their value for a 40-person company stretching a $680,000 launch.

Social-media campaigns aimed at learners: Social ads can reach large numbers cheaply and build learner pull-through, reinforced by the 40% who first heard of ZYL through social media. Results are measurable and the content can show improved completion rates from 64% to 71%. The drawback is that learners are often not the buyers: colleges and employers hold the budgets, so awareness may not convert into the 70,000-unit subscription base.

Employer partnerships: Partnering with employers to offer staff training puts ZYL directly in front of organisations that buy licences, and demonstrates adaptive assessments in a real workplace. It builds long-term contracts and recurring revenue, which suits a platform funded by a $420,000 loan. The weakness is that partnerships take time to negotiate and depend on a few large clients, so growth is slower than a broad campaign.

Recommendation: ZYL should choose employer partnerships. They reach the actual buyers, support the 63% upgrade intention found in the survey, and create the recurring subscriptions needed to justify the $680,000 platform. Social-media campaigns are rejected because they target learners rather than the colleges and employers who pay, and trade journals are rejected as slow, narrow and unable to demonstrate the product; ZYL should use modest social advertising to support, not replace, the partnership strategy.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of ZYL with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of ZYL with a well-justified recommendation explaining why journals and social campaigns are rejected.

questions.question_text: ZYL has content-error complaints and labour turnover of 11% among instructional designers. Explain two benefits for ZYL of introducing profit sharing.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Profit sharing gives ZYL's 40 employees a direct financial stake in the platform's success, motivating designers to reduce the content errors still reported by colleges and to support the move from a 64% to a 71% completion rate. Because rewards depend on profit, staff have an incentive to protect the $5.60 contribution per unit and the $10.60 price rather than simply complete tasks, which helps justify the $680,000 investment.

Point 2: A share of profits can improve retention and reduce the 11% labour turnover among instructional designers by making them feel valued and rewarded for the 19 content errors a month they are working to eliminate. Retaining experienced designers preserves the knowledge behind the adaptive-assessment content, protects the 70,000-unit subscriber base and avoids repeated recruitment during the launch, which is especially important in a flat, democratic team where each specialist carries significant responsibility. Profit sharing also links rewards to the 71% completion target, giving designers a clear reason to improve content quality.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ZYL's content errors, turnover and profit.

questions.question_text: ZYL must upskill 22 engineers to build the AI-tutoring platform. Consider on-the-job training on the tutoring codebase or off-the-job AI certification at $1,100 per employee. Which should ZYL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Weekly pairing on ZYL's own tutoring codebase keeps all 22 engineers working on real content and assessment tasks, costs no fees and teaches the exact adaptive-assessment logic behind the $680,000 platform. It fits a flat team of 40 already dealing with 11% designer turnover and content-error complaints, and it protects the 98.9% uptime subscribers expect. Its weaknesses are that senior engineers lose delivery time, bad habits can spread, and no external certificate is earned, which matters when colleges ask for evidence of AI expertise.

Off-the-job certification: The tech college's AI course at $1,100 per employee provides structured, current skills and a recognised qualification for all 22 engineers, costing $24,200 — modest beside the $680,000 investment. However, it removes 22 people from development during the launch, delays the platform, and the content is generic, so ZYL still needs in-house follow-up on its own codebase once the course finishes.

Decision: ZYL should choose on-the-job training as the main method, with off-the-job certification for four lead engineers. It is cheaper, immediate and specific to the product, protects the work on content errors and adaptive assessments, and reduces turnover by keeping staff engaged. Full off-the-job certification for all 22 is rejected because it removes most of the engineering team at launch, spends $24,200 on generic content and delays a platform being sold to colleges and employers; certification can be extended later once the system is stable. With 98.9% uptime and 19 content errors a month to handle, ZYL needs its engineers on the product during launch.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to ZYL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of ZYL.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of ZYL with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and platform relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how ZYL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $10.60 − $5.00 = $5.60. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.60.

Formula: Margin of safety = Current output − Break-even output. Break-even = $252,000 ÷ $5.60 = 45,000 units, so substitution: 70,000 − 45,000 = 25,000 units. Answer: margin of safety is 25,000 units a year.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways ZYL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Break-even of 45,000 units against 70,000 units sold gives a margin of safety of 25,000 units, so ZYL can lose subscribers while fixing content errors and still cover $252,000 of fixed costs.
2. Contribution of $5.60 helps managers test a discount for colleges taking multiple licences: a 5% price cut to $10.07 would reduce contribution to $5.07 and raise break-even towards roughly 49,700 units, showing whether extra volume compensates.
3. The $420,000 bank loan can be stress-tested against the 45,000-unit break-even point, ensuring subscription revenue stays high enough to service debt before further spending on the $680,000 platform.
4. Average total cost of $8.60 a unit ($252,000 ÷ 70,000 = $3.60, plus $5.00) benchmarks the new platform: reducing content errors and raising completion rates lowers unit cost, while the 10.2% hosting-cost rise threatens to push it up.

questions.model_answer: (i) Contribution per unit = $5.60 | (ii) Margin of safety = 25,000 units | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: 25,000-unit safety margin versus 70,000-unit output; discount modelling against the $10.60 price; stress-testing the $420,000 bank loan; and unit-cost benchmarking at $8.60 against content errors and 10.2% hosting inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate ZYL's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has ZYL's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 42.3%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.5%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 18.0%
ROCE 2024 = 10.0%
ROCE 2025 = 13.4%

Detailed workings: 2024 — revenue $1,420,000 − cost of sales $820,000 = gross profit $600,000; 600 ÷ 1,420 × 100 = 42.3%. Operating profit $213,000 ÷ revenue $1,420,000 × 100 = 15.0%. Operating profit ÷ capital employed $2,130,000 × 100 = 10.0%. 2025 — revenue $1,760,000 − cost of sales $960,000 = gross profit $800,000; 800 ÷ 1,760 × 100 = 45.5%. Operating profit $317,000 ÷ revenue $1,760,000 × 100 = 18.0%. Operating profit ÷ capital employed $2,360,000 × 100 = 13.4%.

Evaluation: Profitability improved on each measure. The gap between sales and direct costs widened from 42.3% to 45.5%, helped by falling content errors (19 a month) and better completion rates; the bottom-line measure widened from 15.0% to 18.0% as revenue grew faster than capital employed; and returns on capital rose from 10.0% to 13.4%, showing the tutoring investment has been used effectively so far. The main qualifications are that interest payable rose from $17,000 to $28,000, so debt service takes more operating profit, and the 2025 result depends on retaining 22 engineers amid 11% designer turnover and converting the 560 surveyed learners and tutors, only 63% of whom intend to upgrade, while hosting costs rise 10.2%.

Conclusion: ZYL's profitability has improved. All three measures rose (42.3% to 45.5%, 15.0% to 18.0%, 10.0% to 13.4%) through wider margins and better use of capital rather than extra borrowing. ZYL should defend the gain by fixing the loan rate and holding the $5.60 contribution per unit as the $680,000 platform scales.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, operating profit, interest and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether ZYL's profitability improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ZYL of using automated content-error checking for its e-learning materials.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Automated checking can catch mistakes before learners see them, reducing the content errors still reported at 19 a month and protecting the improvement in completion rates from 64% to 71%. Reliable material supports the $10.60 price and $5.60 contribution, strengthens the case for the $680,000 AI-tutoring platform, and helps satisfy the 54% of 560 surveyed learners and tutors who value adaptive assessments.

Disadvantage: The checking software adds to the $252,000 fixed costs or the $5.00 variable cost per unit, squeezing margins unless the 63% who intend to upgrade actually subscribe. Automated checks may also miss conceptual errors that need a skilled instructional designer, and with 11% designer turnover ZYL still needs people to interpret results; false alarms could divert the 22 engineers from building the platform and leave the $420,000 loan-funded launch behind schedule. With 63% of the 560 surveyed learners intending to upgrade, ZYL must show that checking improves material rather than delaying it.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to ZYL's content quality, costs and staffing.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.2% rise in hosting and bandwidth costs will affect ZYL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If ZYL's $420,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point increase adds 0.75% × $420,000 = $3,150 a year, small beside $252,000 of fixed costs and largely avoidable by fixing the rate. Higher rates might deter some college spending, but Appendix 3 shows e-learning spending still growing 12.3%, so the direct cash effect is modest.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, from $12.35 to $13.14): Each affected hour costs $13.14 − $12.35 = $0.79 more, equal to 6.4% × $12.35 = $0.79. The insert gives no hours worked or pay rates by worker, so an annual wage bill cannot be honestly calculated; the defensible point is that support wages rise unavoidably, and with 11% designer turnover ZYL may spend more on recruitment and $1,100 certification of replacements.

Hosting and bandwidth costs (up 10.2%): Streaming AI tutoring runs on hosting inside the $5.00 variable cost and underpins the 98.9% uptime. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a labelled upper bound is defensible: if the whole $5.00 rose 10.2%, that would add 0.102 × $5.00 = $0.51 per unit, or 70,000 × $0.51 = $35,700 a year, cutting the $5.60 contribution towards about $5.09. Even a fraction of that applies to every subscription and cannot be removed by fixing a loan.

Conclusion: The 10.2% hosting and bandwidth rise will have the greatest impact. It recurs across all 70,000 units, hits the cost line that delivers tutoring and uptime, and is greater than the 5.5% technology-inflation rate, so recovery through price rises is limited given the survey shows only 63% intend to upgrade. The wage rise is second because it lifts payroll but cannot be quantified from the insert, and the interest rise is smallest and fixable — both still require cost discipline while the $680,000 platform launches.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to ZYL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on ZYL's costs, prices or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes with a justified judgement that hosting cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
